citation: Fiona Chen and James Stratton (both Harvard University), 'Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production', job market paper, current version November 19, 2026 (first version January 7, 2026). PDF: https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf (122 pages). Not found on NBER (NBER w35275 is a different paper) and the arXiv ID I tried (2606.15960) is also a different paper; SSRN/arXiv listing not confirmed [uncertain].
source_tier: Working paper / job market paper, not peer reviewed (author-hosted PDF)
access_status: Fully read (author-hosted PDF downloaded and text-extracted; intro, section 5, conclusion, appendix quotes checked). Not read in full: model and appendix sections.
sponsor_and_incentive: Data is proprietary from Jellyfish, an engineering analytics vendor that sells measurement of engineering teams (a commercial interest in AI-impact metrics). Funding per the paper: Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship; Harvard Kennedy School Stone Program; Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program. Paper states conclusions are the authors' not Jellyfish's, and Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only for disclosure of proprietary information, not scientific content. exact_quotes: Abstract: "AI substantially increases code output but has small effects on final software output and no detectable effect on employment. Code review becomes the bottleneck. Code waits longer to reach a reviewer, spends longer in active review, and receives more requested changes."
Abstract: "covering 445M work events — GitHub coding activity, Jira issues, and Google Calendar events — for 720,542 workers at 655 firms."

Introduction: "after adoption of AI agents, the average time from the code's review submission to its merge increases by 56.1%. This change represents both an increase in the time that code waits in a 'backlog,' by 59.9%, and an increase in the time after code has begun active review, by 58.5%."
Introduction: "79.1% of firms have adopted AI code review tools, but still largely keep humans in the loop, with the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments being written by humans."
Section 5.2: "AI agents significantly lengthen the review process, by 1.99 days, or 56.1% of the baseline mean of 3.56 days."
Section 5.2: backlog "by 1.67 days, or 59.9% of the baseline mean of 2.78 days, and ... active review, by 2.33 days, or 58.5% of the baseline mean of 3.98 days."
Conclusion: "Code review explains much of this gap." (gap between PRs +35.7% and Jira issues +13.7%)

Interview, junior engineer (appendix and intro): "People could make a huge number of commits quickly, but code review was still the bottleneck. ... After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks."

Interview, senior engineer (appendix): "If you speed up coding, the bottleneck shifts somewhere else. ... the real bottleneck has been communication between business and product teams, as well as review and QA."
Conclusion: "As one stage of production speeds up, the bottleneck shifts to another, and labor must be reallocated towards it."
key_claims: Paper exists, by Chen and Stratton. Staggered difference-in-differences (event study) on firm adoption of two generations of AI coding tools. Assistants (Copilot-style) raise code output moderately; agents raise it more. Final output (resolved Jira issues/epics) rises far less, and employment shows no detectable change. Review is identified as the bottleneck: after agent adoption code waits longer for a reviewer (capacity constraint) and spends longer in active review with more comments (consistent with lower quality of code entering review). Reviewers are not interchangeable: they review code they know (82.8% of reviews vs 17.2% if random) and senior code is mostly reviewed by seniors (75.7%) vs junior code (32.8%). AI review tools do not remove the bottleneck: 79.1% of firms used them by July 2026, but only 23.3% of review comments are AI-generated and 10.8% of PRs get an AI comment. Calibrated model: agents raise coding productivity 73.7%, slightly lower review productivity (-7.0%), firms shift labour from coding (-22.7%) to review (+43.4%). Long run: output +16.1% and employment -13.2% once firms adjust; if review productivity does not keep pace, output +57.8% by 2031, if it does, up to +341.4% output and up to -76.2% employment. Implication stated: measure the whole production process, and invest in complementary organisational changes.
headline_figures: 445M work events, 720,542 workers, 655 firms, Jan 2021 to Aug 2026 (abstract). Matches lead (445 million). The earlier August version reportedly had 718 firms and ~300M events (secondary coverage, not opened) [uncertain].

56.1%: rise in average days from PR submission to merge after AI agent adoption (+1.99 days on baseline mean 3.56). Matches lead in number, but the paper says 'to its merge' (section 5.2/intro); a secondary article (beri.net) described it as 'to approval'. Compared with pre-adoption baseline, staggered DiD; AI assistants show no significant effect.
59.9%: rise in backlog wait before review starts (+1.67 days on baseline 2.78). Matches lead.
58.5%: rise in active review time (+2.33 days on baseline 3.98). Matches lead. Footnote: baseline means do not sum to the overall baseline.
35.7%: rise in PRs opened after agent adoption (12 months after adoption, per intro; extra effect of agents); lines of code +44.0%, commits +36.0%. Assistants: LOC +30.4%, commits +16.8%, PRs +20.9%.
13.7%: rise in Jira issues resolved from agents (borderline significant; can rule out increases above 30.7%); epics +18.0%; assistants -1.5% issues, +3.4% epics.

Review intensity: share of code changes with at least one review comment +13.1%; comments per change +38.6%; share of PRs formally blocked +1.07 pp (38.5% of 2.77% baseline), marginally insignificant.
Engineers spend 30 to 40% of time writing code (Prolific survey of 100 engineers plus external estimates); interviews with 21 workers.
sample_and_method: Proprietary Jellyfish telemetry: GitHub, Jira, Google Calendar, plus firm- and worker-level usage of GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code. 445M events, 720,542 workers, 655 firms, Jan 2021 to Aug 2026. Observed behaviour, not self-report (except 21 interviews and a 100-person Prolific survey used for colour). Staggered difference-in-differences event study using firm adoption timing, with robustness to modern staggered estimators, plus IV for worker take-up. Effects measured roughly 12 to 16 months post adoption. Sample is mostly medium-to-large established firms.
limitations: Stated: short-run (12 to 16 months) so employment may respond slowly; partial equilibrium only (business-stealing could hide negative general equilibrium employment effects); sample largely medium-to-large established firms, may not hold for start-ups; imperfect observation of individual take-up; unobserved confounders may remain; larger firms adopted earlier (controlled). Visible to a careful reader: not peer reviewed; proprietary data cannot be replicated; vendor partner has commercial interest; time-to-merge conflates queueing and quality and says nothing about whether longer review improved quality; Jira issue counts are a noisy output proxy (authors attempt size adjustment with LLM labels); review-productivity decline is inferred from a model, not observed; the long-run predictions (e.g. up to 341.4% output) are model simulations, not measurements. Note the 56.1% is a rise in average merge time versus a firm's own baseline, not a comparison of agent PRs against human PRs.
what_a_leader_can_do: Source supports: measure the whole pipeline (issues shipped, not lines or PRs), and reallocate people and capacity toward review as coding speeds up; the paper's model shows firms already shift labour from coding to review (+43.4%). It also supports expecting that AI review tools alone do not fix it (humans stay in loop, AI writes 23.3% of comments), that reviewer expertise is scarce (single-approver and senior-approval rules after outages created extra queues), and that policies like senior sign-off for AI code lengthen queues. Evidence strength: observational but large and quasi-experimental for the existence of the bottleneck; weak for which specific management interventions work, since the paper tests none. Its implication about 'complementary organisational investments' is stated, not tested.
overlap_with_site_essays: Strong overlap with the premise of The Verification Gap and Checking Isn't Catching (review is where AI output piles up; AI review tools do not replace humans). Relevant to What It Takes to Trust Agent Output (outages leading to senior-approval rules; longer active review and more comments suggest lower quality entering review). Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part: review intensity up (comments per change +38.6%) and review labour +43.4% supports the load on reviewers. I did not open the site essays' text, so overlap is inferred from their titles only [uncertain].
